aroe La. Aug 12—"Bob"
Monroe, La., Aug. 12.—"Bob" Jones, a negro brakeman on the Iron Mountain Railroad, who asaulted Conductor Haddon, of that road Wednesday, was shot and dangerously wounded last night at 12 o'clock by a posse that had been searching for the negro since the assault. Jones was located in a house near the Planters' Oil Mill, and was shot while attempting to make his escape. It is said he fired on the posse as he ran from the house. His chances of recovery are small.

ALEXANDRIA AFFAIRS
REPORTS ON CONDITION OF THE
OLD BRADDOCK HOUSE.
Officially Stated to Be Insanitary and Unsafe—General and Personal News.
Special Correspondence of The Star.
ALEXANDRIA Va. August
ALEXANDRIA, Va., August 23, 1905.

Reports as to the condition of the old Braddock House on North Fairfax street have been received by Mayor Paff from the several city officials who recently, in company with the mayor, made an inspection of the building in response to numerous complaints alleging it to be insanitary and unsafe. According to the expressed opinion of the officials the complaints were well founded.

Health Officer Gorman considers the building insanitary, and the opinion of Secretary Downham of the fire department is that the structure is a veritable fire-trap. While not holding that the building is a menace to life, City Engineer Dunn states that it is in very bad shape.

Letters from the owners of the property stating that they have in prospect an early sale have been received by Corporation Attorney Boothe. It is understood that they will be given a reasonable time in which either to sell or improve the building before any further action is taken.

Colored Youths Arrested.

Four colored youths were arrested yesterday near Four-Mile Run, in Alexandria county, and conveyed to the county courthouse on Fort Meyer Heights, where they were placed in jail to await a hearing on the charge of abusive language and disorderly conduct at the residence of Mr. McDonald, near St. Asaph. During Mr. McDonald's absence, it is stated, several negroes went to his house and demanded something to eat from his wife. They became very threatening and abusive, and Mrs. McDonald hastily barred the doors against them. To the alarm which she gave Mr. McDonald and others responded, and four of the suspects were caught after a long chase. One who resisted was badly beaten in the face, several of his teeth being knocked out. Justice Burrell was notified and will give the prisoners a hearing this afternoon.

The occurrence gave rise to the report here that a criminal assault had been attempted in the county, but it was stated at the courthouse this morning that no charge of that character had been lodged against the prisoners.

General Matters.

Mr. George Davis, a resident of Fairfax county, died yesterday at his home near Riverside, a few miles from this city. His wife and three children survive him. He was an engineer by trade and was about thirty years of age. The remains will be forwarded tomorrow morning to his former home at Woodbridge, Prince William county, for interment.

The funeral of Charles B. Davis, whose death occurred Monday, took place this afternoon from the home of his father, Mr. L. Morgan Davis, 420 North Alfred street. Rev. J. A. Jeffers of the Methodist Episcopal Church conducted the services and the interment was in Bethel cemetery.

Mayor Paff has decided to be at his new office in the Royal street wing of the city hall from 11 to 12 a.m. every day for the transaction of municipal business.

Gracie D. Thomas, the three-year-old daughter of Mr. T. J. Thomas, died last night at the Alexandria Hospital.

Miss Lizzie Slaymaker, who has been visiting at the home of Mrs. Charles Towson in Falmouth, has returned to this city.

JERSEY POSSE FOILED.
Wanted to Lynch Negro Who Attacked Girl.
Somerville, N. J. Aug. 5.—The inhabitants of Franklin Park and Millstown were greatly excited last night when an alarm was given that a negro, Francis Smith, who was employed on the farm of Jacob S. Suydam, a wealthy citizen, had attempted to assault Suydam's daughter Adeline, fifteen years old. The negro entered her room about 10 o'clock by removing the screen from the window and attempted to stifle her with a pillow. Another occupant of the room, Miss Huff, twelve years old, was aroused by the scuffle and struck the negro with the screen, cutting a deep gash in his forehead, at the same time calling for help. The cries were responded to by Miss Suydam's grandfather, Laurence J. Suydam, seventy years old. The negro made his escape and a posse scoured the neighborhood for him. He was discovered in a barn about 4 o'clock this afternoon and narrowly escaped being lynched. Robert Henderson, of the Somerville police, brought the prisoner here, where he was taken before Justice Kitchen, who held him for the grand jury.

Court Proceedings-Bivens Case Mistrial.
Court adjourned Friday night. The case of most interest was that against H. J. Bivens, who while constable of Monroe township, shot and killed a negro who had been beating a ride on the train and ran when Bivens tried to arrest him. The jury took this case at 3 o'clock Friday afternoon and after staying out until 10:30 failed to agree, and a mistrial was ordered. In this case the charge was manslaughter. The defence took the line of argument, introducing proof to that effect, that the ball which killed Furgeson was not fired by Bivens, but by some unknown by-stander. It was proved that the first two shots that he fired were fired into the ground, and he swore that the other two were. The defence also offered proof that the bullet which killed the man was not the same kind used by Bivens, and that the powder was not the same kind. There was an excursion crowd at the depot the morning of the shooting and the theory was advanced that some one who had a pistol, hearing Bivens shooting and seeing the man running, fired also, with the fatal result.

NEGRO HOME BURNED.
Henry Jenkins Believes His House Was Set Afire.
Henry Jenkins Believes His House Was Set Afire.

Fire, believed to have been of incendiary origin, completely destroyed a one-story frame dwelling house, situated just across the county line near Jefferson avenue and Nineteenth street, last night at 11 o'clock. An alarm of fire was sent in to the city fire department and East End company No. 2 responded, but the laddies were unable to extinguish the flames as the building could not be reached by the hose.

The house was owned by Henry Jenkins, a negro carpenter, who, with his wife and four children, were asleep in the building when the fire started. Jenkins was aroused by the smoke and succeeded in getting his family out of the building before it became enveloped in the flames.
Jenkins stated after the fire that several people had made thrats to burn his hom and that he believes one or all of them carried out their threats last night. The negro said that he estimated the loss at $300 and that there was no insurance.

john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A2:
NEGRO LYNCHED BY MOB.
Taken from Jail. Hanged and Riddled with Bullets.
New-Berne, N. C., Aug. 27.—John Moore, a negro, twenty years old, was taken from Craven County jail in this city to-day and lynched by a mob of one hundred masked men armed with rifles and revolvers.

With his hands tied behind him, the negro was led to Neuse River bridge, hanged to one of its braces and his body riddled with bullets.

Moore entered the country store of George Eubank at Clarks, seven miles from New-Berne, last Friday, when the proprietor's wife was the only one there. The negro attempted robbery and struck Mrs. Eubank on the head with a meat axe, fracturing bones and inflicting injuries which, if they do not prove fatal, will at least cause disfigurement for life.

Mrs. Eubank screamed and the negro fled, but was captured in a swamp.

Charlotte, N. C., Aug. 27.—A dispatch from Newbern to "The Observer" says that the real cause of the lynching was that at his preliminary hearing yesterday Moore's bond was fixed at only $300. The lynching was denounced from all the pulpits of the town this morning.
john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A4:
NEGRO HANGED TO BRIDGE.
Only Fifty Men in Lynchers' Mob at Newbern.
About fifty farmers from Clark, a little place near Newbern, N. C., went to the jail at Newbern Sunday morning at 1:30 o'clock and took from there John Moore, a negro who on last Friday viciously assaulted Mrs. George T. Eubanks with a meat ax, and hanged him to one of the cross-bars of the bridge over the Neuse river on Craven street. The mob then riddled his body with bullets. The negro went to the post office at Clark, last Friday afternoon and, finding no one in the office but Mrs. Eubanks, the postmistress, he demanded that he be given money. She turned as if to grant the request, when the brute picked up a meat ax, striking her in the head with it, breaking her jaw and cutting a long gash in her face. He then fled. The neighborhood was aroused and a number of men, the husband among them, gave pursuit. The negro was caught and lodged in jail. He was tried the next day and recommitted to jail in default of only a $300 bond. The Clark people were indignant that the bond should be made so light, and Saturday night they went to Newbern with the purpose of lynching the negro. They met the Newbern sheriff on the street and demanded, at the point of a pistol, that he give them the keys. When they were informed that Jailer Williams had the keys the mob went to the jail and forced him to give the negro up.
john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A6:
NEGRO IS STRUNG UP
MOB GETS IN SUMMARY WORK AT NEWBURN. N. C.
John Moore, Who Beat White Woman Over Head With Meat Axe, Will Not Commit Another Such Deed in Future.
Newburn, N. C., Aug. 27.—John Moore, a negro, 20 years old, was taken from Craven County jail, in this city, early today and lynched by a mob of one hundred masked men armed with revolvers and rifles.

With his hands tied behind him, the negro was led out about a third of a mile from the jail to the draw of Neuse River bridge, hanged to one of its braces and his body riddled with bullets.

The mob attacked the jail between 1 and 2 o'clock this morning. Entrance to the jail was effected by forcing the jailer to surrender the keys. As soon as the attack was discovered, the naval reserves were called out to attempt to prevent the lynching. Crowds rushed to the bridge. Sheriff J. W. Biddle was quickly on the scene, pleading that Moore be left to the law, but his efforts were unavailing, and the mob carried out its plans.

Moore entered the country store of George Eubanks at Clarks, seven miles from Newburn, last Friday, when the proprietor's wife was the only one in the store. The negro attempted robbery and struck Mrs. Eubanks on the head with a meat axe, fracturing some bones and inflicting injuries which, if they do not prove fatal, will at least cause not only disfigurement, but lifelong suffering. Mrs. Eubanks screamed and people came to her rescue. The negro fled, but was captured in a swamp after a chase of a few miles ,and was placed in jail.
john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A15:
Dead Eyes Glare Sightless into Its Depths.
AND THE BODY SWAYS
John Moore, Who Assaulted Mrs. Eubanks, Taken by Mob From Jail at Pistol's Point, Hanged at Neuse River Bridge and Filled With Bullets.
(Special to News and Observer.) New Farm N. C. Aug. 28 John

New Bern, N. C., Aug. 28.—John Moore, the negro who brutally assaulted the wife of Postmaster George T. Eubanks, at Clark's, with a meat axe, was taken out of Craven county jail at 1:30 p. m. Sunday morning and lynched. The mob was composed mostly of countrymen, neighbors of Eubanks, but there were citizens of New Bern in the crowd.

The farmers arrived in town about midnight. They did not make any demonstration until after one o'clock.

Sheriff Biddle, who had been notified that an attempt to get Moore was about to be made, went out on the street to prevent the affair, and was met by a few men, one of whom pointed a revolver at him and said: "Sheriff Biddle, we like you and mean you no harm, but if you go a step further we will kill you. We want the keys to the jail; we are here for a purpose and mean to accomplish it."

Biddle told them he did not have the keys, that Jailer Williams had them. They kept guard over the sheriff and returning to the jail gathered around it and called Williams out on the porch. The men demanded the keys, and upon his refusal to surrender them, held him up at the point of the revolver, secured the keys and made entrance to the jail without making any undue noise or disturbance. The number around the jail at that time did not exceed fifty men.

The Mob Too Quick for Them.

During this episode the alarm had been sounded, and the Naval Reserves and the cutter crew were summoned to guard the jail, but the farmers were too quick and had made away with the man.

The general alarm, ten strokes of the bell, announced to the public that something extraordinary was taking place, and almost immediately the streets were filled with people. Having got possession of Moore they hurried him off to Neuse Bridge, hauling him roughly up Craven street to the river, about a half mile distant. Here they hanged him from one of the iron cross pieces of the draw portion of the bridge, which is located at the New Bern end. After he had been hanged his body was riddled with bullets, at least fifteen bullet holes were seen in it.

The terrible execution accomplished, the mob dispersed. They made no noise during the whole affair and the generalship was perfect.

Thought the Bond Too Small.

The event, deplorable as it is, was the result, not of sudden hot-headedness, but of long and serious meditation, and it is said that if the bond under which Moore was placed, at his preliminary examination had been made a larger amount the thing would never have happened. Justice Barrington made the amount of the bond only $300, an act which enraged the farmers greatly, and they determined to take the law in their own hands, feeling that under the circumstances the law could not make the penalty fit the crime. This statement is made more prominent by the fact that the neighbors kept Eubanks himself from shooting Moore at the time of his arrest, Friday afternoon, and urged him to allow the law to take its course. The men brought Moore to the city and delivered him to the sheriff. It is presumed that the parties of the rescue and the lynching are at least a portion of them identical.

Moore's victim is reported as improving. Dr. Street states that unless blood poison sets in she has a chance to recover, but that she will always suffer from the wound and will always be disfigured. The bones of the face and jaw bone are broken and the wound varies from an inch to an inch and a half in depth. The deed is looked on in different lights today mostly commendatory of the mob's work.

The ministers in the churchese referred to the awful crime and expressed horror and indignation that such a thing should have been committed in New Bern.

They term it an act of barbarism that should not be allowed to go unpunished. They express the hope that deep and full investigation will be made that the guilty men, at least the leaders, may be discovered and brought to justice.

Negroes Approve the Deed.

The News and Observer reporter interviewed colored men on the subject, and without exception, found that they approved of the lynching. Some of the strongest witnesses against Moore were among men of his own race. Those who approved of the lynching were not the low or rowdy sort, but men well thought of in the community and standing high among their people. They believe the deed will have a lasting impreession on the race. There is a disposition here among
john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A16:
those who disapprove of the act to criticise Sheriff Biddle severely for not resisting the lynchers more, but the officer did all within his poweer and an attempt to defend the prisoner would have been useless and doubtless another murder would have been committed. Jailer Williams was helpless in the hands of so many men who could overpower him if it were necessary.

The failure to put a guard around the jail is considered the worst lack of forethought on the part of the sheriff and the greatest source of censure.

It is intimated that plans of the lynching had been devised long before nightfall, and that as far as was possible the way was prepared for the speedy execution. It is said that people knew that this lynching would be attempted as early as five o'clock in the evening. This, however, is not clearly proved. It was thought by the authorities that the excitement over the assault had died away and that the prisoner was safe.

The body was removed at an early hour this morning and placed in jail to await the coroner's inquest, which was held at noon. The verdict was that Moore came to his death by gunshot wounds at the hands of persons unknown to the jury.

The reason for this verdict instead of death by hanging, was that unless death was caused by strangulation it is more probable that he was shot to death as his neck was not broken.

Moore was a very black negro, aged about twenty, of vicious and sullen aspect. He was a stranger in this part of the country and believed to be a tramp, although he was well dressed and had a little money. He said in his trial that he lived in Dover, but as he had previously named two or three other towns as his home he cannot be placed anywhere. He had been employed in the Blades saw mill, but had left that, and at the time of his crime was not working.

Having no friends to take charge of the remains they were buried at the county's expense.
john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A17:
Gov. Glenn Orders Inquiry Into Lynching.
Gov. Glenn of North Carolina did not learn until yesterday of the lynching of John Moore at Newbern Saturday night. He immediately ordered State Solicitor Morrow to hasten to Newbern and thoroughly investigate the lynching, with the object of bringing the lynchers to punishment. The governor, in his instructions to Solicitor Moore, said:

"It is a deplorable and horrible affair, to be condemned by good citizens. It casts a blot on North Carolina and should be severely punished. As announced in my inaugural address, I hold myself ready in all such emergencies to order special terms; therefore there is no excuse for any mob taking the law in its hands and committing the detestable crime of lynching. A mob, carried away by frenzy on account of an unnamable crime, sometimes excuses itself on this account and asks the public not to too severely condemn it. But what excuse can be rendered in this case, where the defendant could have been condignly punished by the courts. For the state's good name, a most searching investigation must be made and due punishment imposed. You will have my cordial help in all your undertakings."
john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A19:
MORE RIGID COMPLIANCE WITH LAW NEEDED.
It is stated that the reason for the recent lynching in North Carolina was the fact that the court held the criminal who attempted murder when thwarted of robbery in the sum of only $300. The woman whom he attacked with the ax is mutilated for life, even if she survives the horrible wound on her neck and face, and for this the negro is held in the sum of $300 to stand his trial, should the grand jury indict. Upon this fact becoming known the gathering of the neighbors followed, the midnight raid on the jail and the lynching of the assailant. For lynching under any circumstances The Light has no apology, but it has less to the judge who would put a man under such nominal bond for such an aggravated and murderous assault. The strongest upholders of law everywhere are of the opinion, again and again expressed that the laxity of law enforcement is at the bottom of the increasing infractions of law. There is enough in this at least to call for serious enquiry and some expert opinion, for it is the prevailing belief in the best informed circles of this country that the uncertainties of law proceedings in the case of notorious criminals and the lack of the enforcement of law generally is at the bottom of the general law disobediences. That laws are made to be observed goes without saying, and no matter how obnoxious or burdensome or unnecessary a law may be that does not absolve the citizen from his obligation to obey it. The remedy for such laws is not in their being ignored, but in their being faithfully executed, and that execution will speedily lead to their being revoked. Laws are only the expression of the will of the majority, and if they are not then the majority have not exercised their rights as citizens in the making of the laws. There is not a law upon the statute book of any state will remain there over one legislative session unless the people acquiesce in its restrictions. The only remedy is obey the laws. If the laws are obnoxious to the majority repeal them. This is all there is to it. Enforcement of law will not prevent lynching, only as the laws against lynching are enforced, but prompt punishment of crime will lead to a feeling that lynchings are unnecessary and in time they will cease. Enforce the law is the only safeguard. Enforce it against all law breakers, no matter whom, lynchers and those whose crimes call for the punishment of law. Relieve the statute book of unnecessary laws and one generation will see lynching largely a lost art and a respect for law that the present shows no sign of. It must come to this or the burden of crime will be too great to be borne.

john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A28:
MOORE LYNGHED.
A MOB OF ONE HUNDRED OR MORE ENTER JAIL, AND SEIZE PRISONER.
Roughly Carried to Neuse River Bridge And The Body Riddled With Bullets.
At about 1:30 o'clock this morning a mob consisting of about one hundred masked men gathered at the jail, well armed, and at the point of revolvers and rifles the jailer turned over the keys.

The mob entered the jail and seized the negro, John Moore, who assaulted Mrs. George T. Eubanks, at Clarks, Friday, with a meat axe, inflicting injuries from which she will always suffer. The mob dragged him roughly up Craven street to the Neuse river bridge, where he was hanged to the bracings of the draw, and his body riddled with bullets.

The sheriff appeared upon the scene and tried to persuade the mob to let the law take its course, but was held back by the point of revolvers, from approaching the jail.

The fire alarm was sounded and the streets were soon filled with citizens, but too late to prevent the lynching. The coroner was called and viewed the body giving permission to have the body removed.

After the lynching, a rumor was all at that another prisoner in the jail would be taken out and lynched, whereupon the sgeriff notified the commander of toe Naval Reserves, and asked for their assistance.
john-moore-new-bern-1905-08-27.A29:
A Negro Pays the Death Penalty for His Crime.
A Murderous Assault With a Meat Axe on a Lady for Purpose of Robbery—The Fiend Caught and Placed in Jail—Taken out Early Sunday Morning by an Orderly Crowd and Hanged—His Victim's Condition Serious
(New Bern Journal August 26.)

One of the most atrocious attacks that has ever been attempted in this section was made by a negro named John Moore, and claiming LaGrange as his home, at Clarks yesterday. The man was desperate or he would never have made so bold an attempt to rob.

Moore went to the store of George T. Eubanks in Clark which is a general store, yesterday morning about 11 o'clock and demanded some money of Mrs. Eubanks who was keeping store and was temporarily alone. The lady refused to give him any and he told her if she didn't hand over some money and do it—quick he would kill her. She was terribly frightened by him and feared that the man would carry out his threat and started to turn around apparently to get some money for him and while she was facing him he grabbed a meat axe and struck her a terrible blow on the head cutting a gash from the roots of the hair to her neck, fracturing the bones of the head and face and breaking the jaw bone, the wound extended down the neck. She was rendered unconscious and at a late hour last night she was in a critical condition.

After committing the deed the negro ran off without endeavoring to get any money and as he left the store or very shortly therafter the clerk discovered Mrs. Eubanks and quickly raised the alarm. Happily some one observed Moore as he came running out of the store and they noted the way he ran; when it was known what had been done a big crowd of men and boys took after him, Moore coming toward New Bern. He had about five or ten minutes start and was able to get quite a distance away. After running several miles he took refuge in a swamp near the Oaks farm where he was found by some of his pursuers at half past four. Mr. Eubanks had a shot gun with him but refused to use it, although some of his neighbors urged him to do so.

The man was held and his hands tied securely behind his back. Mr. Eubanks brought the man to the city and delivered him to Officer Griffin who turned him over to Sheriff Biddle and he is now in prison.

He was taken before Justice of the Peace Barrington who set his case for trial this morning. Moore protests innocence but his guilt is clear as he was seen loitering around the store a short time before the attack and was seen to run out of the store. He can be positively identified by a half dozen or more persons. He is an evil looking negro and the extreme rigor of the law will be invoked as it was a most unprovoked attack.

TO AVENGE PATIENT'S DEATH
Investigation to Be Held Into Causes of Sudden Demise of Nall.

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

RALEIGH, N. C., September 7.—At the request of Solicitor Moore, of the Superior Court, Judge Purnell has ordered the removal of Dave Bryan, alias "Lightning," a Federal prisoner convicted of counterfeiting, from the jail at Newbern to that at Goldsboro. Bryan was at jail in Newbern with Moore, a negro, who was taken out by a mob and lynched last week.

It is believed by the solicitor that he can give some useful information to the State regarding the lynchers, whom, of course, he saw, and the theory is that he will give information more freely at some other point than at Newbern, where possibly some pressure, such as fear of injury or even death, might be brought to bear upon him. The solicitor laid these facts before the judge, who has ordered the transfer made, and Moore will be thoroughly questioned. One man, charged with being concerned in this lynching, has already been arrested, and the State expects soon to secure other arrests. While there is a good deal of sentiment against this lynching, yet it must be said that there is some in support of it.

CROWD JUMPED ON
Helped Punish Colored Man for Drawing a Knife.
W. M. Herdon, a colored man, was severely beaten by a crowd at First avenue S and Third street at about 1 o'clock this morning, when he attacked a young man with a knife. The two had a dispute and the white man, who was much the smaller, threw Herdon to the ground and was beating him soundly when the crowd that had gathered started in to help him. He then left and the police arrested Herdon on a charge of disorderly conduct.
